This introduction section from a CELREP article discusses the role of inflammasomes in the innate immune response, detailing their composition and function in response to pathogens and tissue damage.

Inflammasomes represent a unique category of multiprotein complexes known for their pivotal role in the innate immune response to pathogenic invasions and tissue damage. 1 , 2 , 3 , A classic inflammasome comprises pattern recognition receptors, the effector protein caspase-1, and the scaffold apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC). 4 5 , Upon activation, these pattern recognition receptors form polymers and subsequently recruit ASC and pro-caspase-1 to assemble into the inflammasome, ultimately activating caspase-1. 6 7 , Once activated, caspase-1 serves a dual function. Firstly, it cleaves proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 precursors, promoting their maturation and subsequent release. Secondly, activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD, releasing its N-terminal active segment. 8 This active segment punctures holes in the cell membrane, triggering cell death known as “pyroptosis.” 9 10 , NLRP3 inflammasome is the best-studied inflammasome, and its excessive activation relates to autoimmune diseases and inflammatory diseases. 11

This introduction section from the article discusses the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) as a key regulator of NLRP3 inflammasome activity through post-transcriptional mechanisms in eukaryotic mRNA.

11 N6-methyladenosine (m 6 A) is the most abundant internal modification in eukaryotic mRNA. 12 , 13 , 14 , In recent years, it has been shown to broadly regulate NLRP3 inflammasome activity at the post-transcriptional level. 15 16 , 17 , 18 , For example, in acute kidney injury, IGF2BP1 recognizes the m 19 6 A site of E2 f 1 mRNA, stabilizes its expression, increases MIF levels, and induces NLRP3-related pyroptosis. Betaine promotes YTHDF2-mediated degradation of 20 Nlrp 3 mRNA, thereby suppressing microglial NLRP3 activation. Lactate-induced ALKBH5 demethylation reduces 21 Nlrp 3 mRNA stability. Meanwhile, WTAP and METTL14 enhance 22 Nlrp 3 mRNA stability through m 6 A modification, aggravating inflammation. 23 , YTHDF1 facilitates the translation of CLOCK and amplifies the NLRP3 signaling pathway through liquid-liquid phase separation. 24 Collectively, these studies indicate that the m 25 6 A “writer-reader-eraser” axis profoundly influences NLRP3 activity in multiple pathological contexts through post-transcriptional regulation. However, it remains unclear whether, during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation, m 6 A also acts in a co-transcriptional manner to regulate chromatin remodeling and nascent RNA transcription, and how the m 6 A marks on nascent RNA are recognized to initiate transcription of inflammasome-related genes. Although previous studies have suggested that METTL3 can influence chromatin states, bind promoter elements, and install m 6 A marks on nascent RNA to directly regulate transcription, 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , it is still unknown whether and how these mechanisms function during macrophage inflammasome activation. Our study focuses on addressing this question. 30

This introduction section from the article discusses the methods used to create an integrated chromatin-transcription-translation map of macrophages during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, emphasizing various sequencing and profiling techniques employed in the research.

30 In this work, we combined chromatin-associated RNA sequencing (chrRNA-seq), chrRNA-MeRIP-seq, kethoxal-assisted single-stranded DNA sequencing (KAS-seq), polysome profiling, RNA-FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) colocalization, and rescue experiments to build an integrated chromatin-transcription-translation map of macrophages during NLRP3 inflammasome activation. We found that, upon inflammatory stimulation, METTL3 installs m 6 A marks on nascent RNA, particularly on Jak1 , Nlrp3 , and Il1β transcripts. Among them, the m 6 A modification on Jak1 is recognized by YTHDF1, which enhances its polysome loading and translation, thereby activating the JAK1-STAT3 pathway and driving C/EBPβ-mediated transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β . In parallel, m 6 A-YTHDF1 directly promotes the translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β mRNAs, further amplifying protein production after transcription initiation. Notably, METTL3 deletion increases global chromatin accessibility and relieves widespread transcriptional repression but selectively reduces the transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β . We interpret this “decoupling” phenomenon using a hierarchical model: under inflammatory stimulation, the METTL3-m 6 A axis regulates global transcriptional activity, while the selective decrease in Nlrp3/Il1β transcription arises from insufficient m 6 A-dependent JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ signaling, which directly determines whether these genes are effectively transcribed. Finally, in myeloid-specific Mettl3 conditional knockout mice and STAT3 inhibitor-treated mice, we confirmed that the METTL3-m 6 A-JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis critically controls NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated inflammation in vivo , as demonstrated in models of sepsis, MSU-induced arthritis, and obesity-related chronic inflammation.

This results section from the study by Jie Fu discusses how METTL3-mediated m6A methylation influences the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, supported by experimental findings from various macrophage models.

### METTL3-mediated m 6 A methylation promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages

To investigate the role of RNA m 6 A modification in macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation, we established NLRP3 inflammasome models in J774A.1 cells and bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). Consistent results from m 6 A immunofluorescence, mRNA m 6 A quantification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and mRNA m 6 A dot blot analysis ( Figures 1 A–1D 6 A modification was markedly increased following inflammasome activation. However, regardless of NLRP3 activation, the expression of m 6 A-related writer, eraser, and reader proteins showed no significant changes ( Figures S1 A–S1D), indicating that the elevated m 6 A level was not caused by altered expression of these enzymes. To identify the major methyltransferase responsible, we generated METTL3- and METTL14-deficient J774A.1 macrophages ( Figures S2 A–S2B) and quantified m 6 A levels. Under LPS + ATP stimulation, METTL3 deletion reduced global mRNA m 6 A levels by approximately 50%, whereas METTL14 deletion caused only about a 20% reduction ( Figure S2 C), suggesting that METTL3 is the dominant m 6 A writer in this context. Furthermore, in Nlrp3 knockout J774A.1 cells, LPS + ATP stimulation did not decrease global m 6 A levels, and the protein expression of METTL3, METTL14, and the demethylase FTO remained comparable to wild-type (WT) cells ( Figures S3 A–S3B). These findings indicate that the increase in m 6 A is independent of NLRP3 activation and more likely represents an upstream regulatory event rather than a downstream consequence.

This results section from the study by Jie Fu discusses how METTL3-mediated m 6 A methylation influences NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages, highlighting the independent role of m 6 A in regulating IL-1β secretion.

These findings indicate that the increase in m 6 A is independent of NLRP3 activation and more likely represents an upstream regulatory event rather than a downstream consequence. At the functional level, we established two independent METTL3-deficient J774A.1 cell lines (sh- Mettl3 #1/#2) ( Figure S2 A). In the LPS + ATP model, METTL3 loss significantly reduced IL-1β secretion in the supernatant and decreased the cleavage of caspase-1 and GSDMD ( Figures 1 E and 1H). In addition, NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β protein levels were notably reduced, whereas pro-IL-18, pro-caspase-1, ASC, and full-length GSDMD were largely unaffected ( Figure 1 E). This inhibitory effect was also observed when NLRP3 was activated by other stimuli, including nigericin and MSU crystals ( Figure 1 K), resulting in decreased NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β expression, reduced caspase-1 cleavage, and lower IL-1β secretion. In primary macrophages, we crossed Mettl3 f/f mice with Lyz2-Cre mice to generate myeloid-specific METTL3-deficient mice (Lyz2-Cre- Mettl3 f/f ) ( Figure S4 A). In both BMDMs and peritoneal macrophages (PMs) from these mice, METTL3 deletion similarly inhibited NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β secretion, consistent with the findings in cell lines ( Figures 1 F–1G and 1I–1J). ASC oligomerization and speck formation are key steps in inflammasome assembly. Under secondary stimulation, METTL3 deficiency markedly impaired ASC oligomerization and speck formation ( Figures 1 L–1N). As a downstream effect, activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to release GSDMD-N, which forms pores in the plasma membrane and triggers pyroptosis. We assessed N-GSDMD accumulation in the membrane fraction and LDH release, and found that METTL3 loss significantly reduced both ( Figures 1 O–1P), suggesting that pyroptosis was suppressed and cell viability improved.

processed_chunks.text:
This results section from the study highlights the essential role of METTL3-mediated m6A modifications in enhancing Il1β and Nlrp3 transcription, thereby contributing to NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages.

These results collectively establish the central role of the METTL3-m 6 A axis in promoting macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation. ### METTL3 enhances Il1β and Nlrp3 transcription through its catalytic m 6 A activity

Our previous results showed that METTL3 deficiency in macrophages markedly reduced NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β protein levels, but had little effect on pro-IL-18, pro–caspase-1, ASC, or full-length GSDMD ( Figure 1 E). To clarify the molecular mechanism underlying this regulation, we systematically examined how METTL3 affects the expression of inflammasome-related genes during NLRP3 activation. Under unstimulated conditions, loss of METTL3 did not alter the mRNA levels of inflammasome-related genes ( Figure 2 Il1β and Nlrp3 were selectively decreased, while Caspase1 , Asc , Il18 , and Gsdmd remained unchanged ( Figure 2 B). To distinguish whether these effects were due to transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulation, we analyzed m 6 A modification and mRNA stability of Il1β and Nlrp3 transcripts during activation. Inflammasome activation markedly increased m 6 A modification on both transcripts in a METTL3-dependent manner ( Figure 2 C). However, actinomycin D chase assays revealed no significant difference in their half-lives between control and METTL3-deficient cells ( Figure 2 D). Furthermore, luciferase reporter assays driven by the Il1β and Nlrp3 promoters showed that METTL3 deficiency significantly reduced reporter activity upon LPS or LPS + ATP stimulation, indicating that the downregulation results from reduced transcriptional activity rather than altered mRNA stability ( Figures 2 E and 2F). To directly test whether METTL3 catalytic activity is required, we re-expressed either wild-type METTL3 or a catalytically inactive mutant (D395A) in sh- Mettl3 J774A.1 cells and in BMDMs from Lyz2-Cre- Mettl3 f/f mice. In both systems, only wild-type METTL3—but not D395A—restored Il1β and Nlrp3 expression, while caspase-1 mRNA remained unaffected ( Figures 2 G–2I and S5 B). These results demonstrate that METTL3 promotes Il1β and Nlrp3 expression in an m 6 A-dependent catalytic manner rather than through non-enzymatic structural functions. Subcellular fractionation and colocalization analyses further showed that METTL3 translocates from the nucleoplasm to the chromatin fraction upon inflammasome activation ( Figure 2 J) and colocalizes strongly with the nuclear speck marker SC-35 ( Figure 2 K), consistent with its role in co-transcriptional m 6 A deposition and transcriptional regulation. Notably, CUT&Tag profiling identified 839 METTL3-bound DNA fragments but showed no enrichment at the Il1β and Nlrp3 promoter regions nor at promoters of other core inflammasome genes ( Figures 2 L–2N). These data suggest that METTL3 does not directly occupy these promoters but instead enhances Il1β and Nlrp3 transcription indirectly through its m 6 A catalytic activity, acting on co-transcriptional or chromatin-associated RNAs.

processed_chunks.subsection_title: METTL3 regulates global dynamic transcription and chromatin accessibility during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation
processed_chunks.text:
This results section from Jie Fu's 2025 article explores how METTL3 influences transcriptional regulation and chromatin accessibility during the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, utilizing chrRNA-seq analysis.

### METTL3 regulates global dynamic transcription and chromatin accessibility during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation

To determine the role of METTL3 in genome-wide transcriptional regulation during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, we activated the inflammasome in sh- Scramble and sh- Mettl3 macrophages. Chromatin-associated RNA (chrRNA) was purified and analyzed by chrRNA-seq ( Figure 3 Figure 3 B), indicating that they represent nascent and incompletely spliced transcripts. At the non-coding level, inflammasome activation changed the expression of 668 long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) ( Figure S6 A), while METTL3 loss had little effect on these changes ( Figure S6 B). Comparative analysis of the nascent transcriptome (coding RNA), inflammasome activation significantly altered the transcription of 1,325 genes ( p adj < 0.05, fold change > 2) ( Figure 3 C); METTL3 depletion caused 221 genes to change significantly ( Figure 3 D). Among them, nascent transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β was selectively reduced ( Figures 3 D and 3E). In contrast, genes such as Asc , Gsdmd , Caspase1 , Nek7 , and Il18 were not affected ( Figure 3 D). Globally, inflammasome activation was accompanied by a broad decrease in nascent transcription ( Figure 3 F). When METTL3 was absent, this suppression was partially relieved ( Figure 3 F). Total RNA-seq results showed a similar trend ( Figure 3 G). 5-ethynyl uridine (EU)-Click-iT labeling confirmed that LPS and LPS+ATP inhibited nascent RNA synthesis ( Figure 3 H). METTL3 deficiency, however, significantly reduced this inhibition ( Figure 3 H). Cross-analysis showed that 37% of the downregulated genes in activated sh- Mettl3 cells were normally upregulated after activation in control cells ( Figure 3 I). These included key inflammatory genes such as Nlrp3 and Il1β . Together, these results indicate that METTL3 participates in the remodeling of global transcriptional activity during inflammasome activation. To test whether this effect depends on METTL3’s catalytic activity, we performed rescue experiments in sh- Mettl3 cells using either wild-type METTL3 or the catalytically inactive mutant D395A. Only METTL3-WT restored nuclear EU signals to near-baseline levels. The D395A mutant and empty vector had no effect. This “WT reversible, mutant ineffective” pattern supports that METTL3 reshapes nascent transcription through its m 6 A catalytic activity ( Figure S6 C). To further assess chromatin changes, we performed KAS-seq to measure genome-wide chromatin accessibility ( Figure 3 K). After inflammasome activation, METTL3-deficient cells showed a global increase in chromatin accessibility ( Figures 3 L–3N). The number of open promoter peaks increased from 2,275 to 3,199 ( Figure 3 O). Separate analyses of promoters and enhancers produced similar results ( Figures S7 A–S7B). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that these differential peaks were related to immune regulation, development, and transcriptional control ( Figures 3 P–3Q). At the gene level, METTL3 loss mainly altered chromatin accessibility at the Nlrp3 and Il1β loci ( Figures 3 R and 3S), while other inflammasome genes were largely unchanged. Combining chrRNA-seq and KAS-seq data, we conclude that METTL3 regulates global chromatin-transcription dynamics and selectively promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription during inflammasome activation.

This results section from the CELREP article discusses how METTL3 regulates global chromatin-transcription dynamics and enhances Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription through the transcription factor C/EBPβ during inflammasome activation in macrophages.

Combining chrRNA-seq and KAS-seq data, we conclude that METTL3 regulates global chromatin-transcription dynamics and selectively promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription during inflammasome activation. ### METTL3 promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription by regulating the transcription factor C/EBPβ

While we have established that METTL3 controls the global dynamic transcription during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation, it remains unclear why METTL3 specifically participates in regulating Nlrp3 and Il1β gene transcription. Many studies have explored the relationship between METTL3 and histones to regulate a series of gene expressions associated with specific phenotypes. However, given the specificity of METTL3’s impact on Nlrp3 and Il1β gene transcription during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, we believe that this specificity may not be related to histones but could be associated with specific transcription factors responsible for Nlrp3 and Il1β gene activation. Upon literature review, we found that the common transcription factors for Nlrp3 and Il1β genes include C/EBPβ and ZFP217 ( Figure 4 C/ebpβ nascent transcripts while having no effect on Zfp217 ( Figure 4 B). Moreover, by analyzing KAS-seq data, we assessed the accessibility of the C/ebpβ and Zfp217 genes. Interestingly, we discovered that METTL3 deficiency significantly reduced the activity of the C/ebpβ gene promoter region while not affecting the transcription activity of Zfp217 ( Figure 4 C). Subsequently, through western blot experiments, we found that METTL3 markedly suppressed C/EBPβ protein expression ( Figure 4 D). Furthermore, we conducted CUT&RUN-qPCR experiments using immunoprecipitation (IP)-level C/EBPβ antibodies. The results showed that NLRP3 inflammasome activation significantly promoted the binding of C/EBPβ to the Nlrp3 and Il1β gene promoter regions ( Figure 4 E). However, this effect was inhibited considerably when METTL3 was absent ( Figure 4 E). To further explore the relationship between METTL3, C/EBPβ, Nlrp3 , and Il1β , we generated C/EBPβ-deficient (sh- C/ebpβ ) cells and observed that C/EBPβ deficiency significantly inhibited the expression of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β ( Figure 4 F). Additionally, we transfected sh- Mettl3 cells with a lentivirus containing the pCDH-C/EBPβ plasmid construct. Through flow cytometry, we selected stable cells that lacked METTL3 but overexpressed C/EBPβ. We found that short hairpin (sh)- Mettl3 -pCDH-C/EBPβ cells completely reversed the phenotypes associated with sh- Mettl3 in NLRP3 inflammasome activation ( Figure 4 G). This reversal included the expression of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β and the cleavage of GSDMD downstream of the NLRP3 inflammasome ( Figure 4 G). Moreover, we also observed that the expression of NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, and the cleavage of GSDMD were still induced in sh- Mettl3 -Pcdh-C/EBPβ cells without stimulation ( Figure 4 G). These findings suggest that METTL3 promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription by regulating the transcription factor C/EBPβ.

This results section from CELREP discusses the role of METTL3 in regulating nascent RNA m6A modification and its impact on Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription through the activation of the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis during NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

These findings suggest that METTL3 promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription by regulating the transcription factor C/EBPβ. ### METTL3 regulates nascent RNA m 6 A modification during NLRP3 inflammasome activation and activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis

Our previous results showed that METTL3 regulates global dynamic transcription during NLRP3 inflammasome activation and promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription in an m 6 A-dependent manner. This Results section from Jie Fu's study discusses how METTL3-mediated m 6 A modifications enhance the translation of Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β mRNA through the action of the m 6 A reader YTHDF1 in macrophages.

These findings indicate that m 6 A modification in specific regions of Jak1 , Nlrp3 , and Il1β transcripts facilitates their translation. YTHDF1 is an m 6 A reader that promotes translation by recruiting ribosomes to m 6 A-modified transcripts. 31 , To confirm its involvement, we generated YTHDF1-deficient cells and performed polysome fractionation using sucrose gradient centrifugation ( 32 Figure 6 E). The overall translation profile was unchanged in METTL3-deficient cells but was markedly reduced in YTHDF1-deficient cells, especially in the heavy polysome fraction (>80S) ( Figure 6 F). Quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis showed that both METTL3 and YTHDF1 deficiency significantly decreased the association of Jak1 , Nlrp3 , and Il1β mRNAs with heavy polysomes ( Figure 6 G). To visualize these interactions, we performed RNA-FISH combined with ribosome (18S rRNA) staining. In cells lacking METTL3 or YTHDF1, spatial colocalization of Jak1 , Nlrp3 , and Il1β mRNAs with ribosomes was markedly reduced ( Figure 6 H), consistent with polysome profiling. These results suggest that METTL3 promotes ribosome loading through an m 6 A-YTHDF1-dependent mechanism. At the molecular level, YTHDF1 mainly enhances translation rather than affecting mRNA abundance. Consistent with this, YTHDF1 deletion did not change Jak1 mRNA levels ( Figure 6 I) but significantly reduced Jak1 mRNA enrichment in polysomes ( Figure 6 G). Consequently, p-STAT3 activation and C/EBPβ expression were decreased, leading to reduced transcriptional induction of Nlrp3 and Il1β ( Figures 6 I and 6J). YTHDF1 recognizes these marks and promotes ribosome recruitment. Enhanced translation of Jak1 transcript activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ signaling pathway, which drives Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription. In parallel, direct m 6 A-YTHDF1-mediated translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β further amplifies protein production. Thus, METTL3 and YTHDF1 cooperate to form a feedforward circuit that links m 6 A-dependent translation with NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

This discussion section from the article by Jie Fu explores the role of the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis in restoring Nlrp3/Il1β expression and inflammasome activation in METTL3-deficient macrophages, highlighting the distinction between mRNA stability and translational efficiency.

Overexpression of C/EBPβ in METTL3-deficient cells fully restored Nlrp3 / Il1β expression and inflammasome activation, demonstrating that the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis is the decisive transcriptional switch for Nlrp3 / Il1β activation. At the translational level, our data distinguish mRNA stability from translational efficiency. Actinomycin D chase assays showed no change in Jak1 , Il1β , or Nlrp3 mRNA stability. However, polysome profiling and RT-qPCR confirmed that loss of METTL3 or YTHDF1 reduced the enrichment of Jak1 , Il1β , and Nlrp3 mRNAs in heavy polysome fractions (>80S). Site-specific mapping by chrRNA-MeRIP-seq and SRAMP prediction identified m 6 A sites in Jak1 (3′UTR), Il1β (3′UTR), and Nlrp3 (CDS). Dual-luciferase and site-directed mutagenesis experiments showed that mutation of these m 6 A sites reduced protein expression. RNA-FISH combined with ribosome staining provided spatial confirmation: in METTL3-or YTHDF1-deficient cells, colocalization of these transcripts with ribosomes was significantly reduced. Together, these findings suggest that YTHDF1 recognizes m 6 A marks and promotes ribosome loading, enhancing translation without altering mRNA stability. Enhanced translation of Jak1 acts as an upstream trigger that activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis, which initiates Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription. Meanwhile, m 6 A–YTHDF1–mediated translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β themselves amplifies protein output, forming a positive feedback loop that drives inflammasome activation.

This discussion section from the article explores how m 6 A–YTHDF1-mediated translation enhances Nlrp3 and Il1β levels, creating a positive feedback loop for inflammasome activation and highlighting the regulation of m 6 A on nascent RNA during inflammation.

Meanwhile, m 6 A–YTHDF1–mediated translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β themselves amplifies protein output, forming a positive feedback loop that drives inflammasome activation. Notably, in our chrRNA-MeRIP-seq analyses, we observed that m 6 A on nascent RNA is upregulated upon inflammatory stimulation and is sensitive to METTL3 depletion, whereas the total m 6 A level on ncRNAs does not significantly decrease after loss of METTL3. We view this not as a contradiction to METTL3’s central role but as evidence for a division of labor in m 6 A deposition across transcriptional systems and substrate classes: under inflammatory conditions, METTL3 likely acts co-transcriptionally on pol II-derived nascent transcripts, while the quantified ncRNA pool is heterogeneous and contains a substantial proportion of pol I/III products whose m 6 A marks are more plausibly maintained by non-METTL3 pathways (e.g., METTL5, ZCCHC4, and METTL16), yielding a strong effect on nascent RNA but a limited effect on bulk ncRNA. 39 , 40 , In addition, an assay-level “offset effect” may operate: MeRIP measures aggregate m 41 6 A, and METTL3 can alter both the copy number of distinct ncRNA subgroups and the per-molecule m 6 A occupancy, so countervailing changes across subgroups may cancel at the total level, obscuring subgroup- or site-specific alterations and producing an apparently unchanged global ncRNA m 6 A signal.

This discussion section from Jie Fu's 2025 CELREP article explores the causal chain linking METTL3's role in m6A modification to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages and its implications for transcriptional and translational regulation.

We visualize a complete causal chain connecting “METTL3→ chromatin→ nascent RNA→ m 6 A→ YTHDF1→ enhanced Jak1 translation → STAT3–C/EBPβ activation→ Nlrp3/Il1β transcription→ amplified Nlrp3/Il1β translation,” and demonstrate how METTL3 orchestrates both global transcriptional remodeling and inflammasome-specific gene activation. From a cellular stress perspective, NLRP3 activation is known to cause K + efflux, mitochondrial injury, and ROS accumulation, leading to integrated stress response activation (eIF2α phosphorylation and CDK9/Pol II-Ser2P decrease) and caspase-1-mediated cleavage of nuclear substrates such as PARP, DNA-PK, and Lamin A. 42 , 43 , These events disrupt transcriptional elongation and chromatin structure, representing a “resource redistribution” strategy under stress. Our findings that METTL3 deletion partially alleviates this global transcriptional repression suggest a buffering role of m 44 6 A-chrRNA coupling in transcriptional control during inflammation.

This discussion section from the article explores how METTL3 deletion influences transcriptional control and alleviates acute and chronic inflammation in myeloid cells, highlighting its role in regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome.

Our findings that METTL3 deletion partially alleviates this global transcriptional repression suggest a buffering role of m 44 6 A-chrRNA coupling in transcriptional control during inflammation. At the in vivo level, our results show that myeloid-specific deletion of Mettl3 can significantly alleviate acute inflammation, such as LPS-induced sepsis and MSU-induced arthritis, and improve chronic inflammation and metabolic phenotypes in the HFD model; in wild-type mice, pharmacological inhibition of STAT3 likewise reduces IL-1β/IL-18, suppresses caspase-1 activation and tissue inflammatory infiltration, and joint swelling is concomitantly reduced. These findings are consistent with previous lines of research indicating that inhibiting macrophage JAK-STAT3 signaling can mitigate LPS-induced organ injury/neuroinflammation and that C/EBPβ is associated with inflammatory amplification. 45 , 46 , 47 , At the same time, some reports found that myeloid 48 Mettl3 deletion can alleviate obesity and inflammatory progression by remodeling immunometabolism. 37 , 49 , Compared with these studies, we obtained cross-model, reproducible 50 in vivo evidence across three types of models—acute (sepsis and sterile arthritis) and chronic (obesity-related low-grade inflammation)—thereby strengthening the feasibility and extrapolative value of targeting the Mettl3 -STAT3-C/EBPβ axis to modulate NLRP3-driven inflammation.

This discussion section from the CELREP article highlights the proposed therapeutic strategy targeting the METTL3–m 6 A axis in inflammation-related diseases while addressing the study's limitations that need to be systematically reinforced.

The “transcriptional drive and translational amplification” model proposed here not only provides a unified explanation for m 6 A–inflammasome interactions but also offers a potential therapeutic strategy by targeting the METTL3–m 6 A–YTHDF1–JAK1–STAT3–C/EBPβ axis in inflammation-related diseases. ### Limitations of the study

This study still has several limitations that require systematic reinforcement. First, based on chrRNA-seq, KAS-seq, chrRNA-MeRIP-seq, and WT/MUT-METTL3 rescue, we proposed a directional model—METTL3 → nascent RNA m 6 A → JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ → Nlrp3/Il1β —to explain the epigenetic decoupling whereby chromatin accessibility increases while Nlrp3/Il1β transcription decreases; however, locus-resolved causal evidence is still lacking. Although we extended the framework of chrRNA m 6 A-mediated feedback on chromatin and transcription to macrophage inflammatory activation for the first time, locus-by-locus validation near 29 Nlrp3/Il1β remains necessary. Accordingly, we will combine long-read sequencing to precisely map m 6 A sites on chrRNAs, perform short-term YTHDC1/NEXT perturbations to assess reader dependence, and integrate KAS-seq, ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, and pol II ChIP-seq, and PRO-seq to readout local accessibility and transcriptional dynamics, while simultaneously monitoring C/EBPβ/p-STAT3 occupancy and Nlrp3/Il1β transcriptional output, thereby upgrading correlation to locus-level causality. Second, the current in vivo evidence for necessity mainly relies on pharmacological STAT3 inhibition, which carries potential off-target and pharmacokinetic limitations; future work should test pathway indispensability in genetic interaction models, including myeloid-specific Stat3 / C/ebpβ conditional knockouts combined with Mettl3 -cKO. Finally, for translation, the METTL3-nascent m 6 A-YTHDF1 → JAK1–STAT3–C/EBPβ axis offers multiple intervention nodes (e.g., inhibiting METTL3 or the YTHDF1-m 6 A interaction, or downstream STAT3), with evaluation of sequential or combination strategies with NLRP3 inhibitors/anti-IL-1 therapy. Priority should be given to myeloid/liver-spleen-enriched delivery and short therapeutic windows to minimize systemic suppression, using IL-1β/IL-18, caspase-1 p20, GSDMD-N, and nuclear p-STAT3 as pharmacodynamic readouts, alongside stratification of populations with high inflammatory burden or metabolic low-grade inflammation, to cautiously advance clinical translation.

This STAR★Methods section from the article details the procedures for CUT&Tag library generation, including the use of specific reagents and protocols for sequencing and analysis of bead-bound cells.

The complete sequence is presented in Table S4 . ### CUT&Tag library generation, sequencing and analysis

CUT&Tag was performed with the Hyperactive In-Situ ChIP Library Prep Kit (Vazyme, TD901) with minor adaptations. Cells were transferred to low-bind 1.5 mL tubes, mixed with 10 μL pre-washed ConA beads (Vazyme N411), and incubated 10 min, RT. Bead-bound cells were incubated in 50 μL Antibody Buffer containing 1 μg anti-METTL3 2h, RT, then washed 2× with 800 μL Digi-wash buffer. A 1 μg secondary antibody in 50 μL Digi-wash was added (45 min), followed by 2 × 800 μL Digi-wash. Next, 100 μL Digi-300 buffer plus 0.58 μL pG-Tn5 was added (1h), samples were washed 2× with Digi-wash, then tagmented in 300 μL Tagmentation Buffer (37°C, 1h). Reactions were stopped by adding 10 μL 0.5 M EDTA +3 μL 10% SDS +2.5 μL Proteinase K (20 mg/mL) and incubating 37°C, 1h. DNA was purified by phenol:chloroform extraction, ethanol-precipitated, air-dried, and resuspended in 25 μL TE. Libraries were PCR-amplified (Vazyme TD204) and sequenced on Illumina HiSeq X Ten/2500 per manufacturer instructions. Raw reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic-0.39 and then mapped to mouse genome (mm10) using bowtie2 (version 2.4.1) with “—dovetail” parameter in default mode: search for the multiple alignments, report the best one. Duplicated reads were removed with samtools “rmdup”. Peaks were called using HOMER in factor style with “-F 2 -L 2 -tagThreshold 10” parameters. Peaks identified in two biological replicates were pooled using bedtools (v.2.26.0) and were used in further analysis. The ENCODE blacklist was downloaded and used to mark CUT&RUN peaks. ROSE identified peaks with high intensity with default parameters. 62

This STAR★Methods section from Jie Fu's 2025 article details the KAS-seq data analysis process, including library sequencing, read trimming, and alignment to the reference genome using specific software tools.

Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (PE150), targeting ∼30 million reads per library. ### KAS-seq data analysis

Low quality and adapter containing reads were trimmed from KAS-seq raw data using trim-galore package. Reads shorter than 80bp were removed. Trimmed reads were aligned to the reference genome (mm10) using bowtie2 (v2.3.3.1) under default parameters. Mapped sam files were subsequently converted and sorted to bam files using samtools sort (v1.9). Duplicates were removed using samtools rmdup (v1.9) to get the unique mapped reads. Bam files were converted to bed files and bedGraph files using bedtools. BedGraph files were then converted to bigWig files using bedgraphtobigwig. Peaks were called using MACS2 (v2.2.7.1) with using broad peaks-call mode under default parameters, except for ‘--broad-cutoff = 0.05’. FDR cut-off of 0.05 was used to determine significant peaks. The ChIPseeker R package was invoked to annotate nearest genes and genomic features to peaks. Differentially peaks were identified by DiffBind with a cut-off value of log2|fold change|>0 and p value < 0.05. The clusterProfiler was used to perform functional enrichment analysis for the annotated significant peaks based on Gene Ontology (GO) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). HOMER(v4.11) was utilized to search for sequence motif among significant peaks. E value cutoff of 0.05 was used to select significantly enriched motifs.

Figure 1: METTL3-mediated m6A methylation increases IL-1β secretion in J774A.1 macrophages, with sh-Mettl3#2 cells showing a significant reduction in IL-1β levels compared to sh-Scramble (p < 0.01). Additionally, METTL3 enhances the transcription of Nlrp3, as demonstrated by increased protein levels of NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, and pro-caspase-1 in LPS and ATP-stimulated J774A.1 cells. These findings establish the critical role of METTL3 in promoting NLRP3 inflammasome activation through upregulation of IL-1β and Nlrp3 transcription.

(D) The mRNA m 6 A dot blot analysis in the CON and LPS + ATP groups of J774A.1 and BMDMs cells. metadata.title: METTL3-mediated m 6 A on nascent RNA coordinates translational and transcriptional programs to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages
metadata.abstract: Fu et al. show that METTL3 installs m 6 A on nascent Jak1 / Nlrp3 / Il1β RNAs to activate the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis, thereby driving NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Myeloid Mettl3 deletion or STAT3 inhibition reduces inflammation in LPS sepsis, MSU arthritis, and HFD-induced obesity models.

These findings underline the crucial role of the METTL3-m6A axis in promoting NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages.
